claim: The infection source for hospital onset COVID-19 infections (HOCIs) cannot always be readily identified based only on epidemiological data.

evidence: This describes the methodology developed in this study.

claim: Transmission of SARS-CoV-2 is possible from asymptomatic or presymptomatic carriers.

claim: In most HOCIs meeting the PHE definition of inclusion within an outbreak event, evidence of clusters of similar viral sequences located on the ward concerned was found.
source: In most HOCIs meeting this definition of inclusion within an outbreak event, we found evidence of clusters of similar viral sequences located on the ward concerned, and the SRT results were in line with available local IPC classifications in the majority of cases.

claim: The SRT results were in line with available local IPC classifications in the majority of cases.
source: In most HOCIs meeting this definition of inclusion within an outbreak event, we found evidence of clusters of similar viral sequences located on the ward concerned, and the SRT results were in line with available local IPC classifications in the majority of cases.

claim: A substantial minority (54/279) of HOCIs assumed to be part of a ward outbreak were isolated cases for which the sequencing data refuted genetic linkage to other sequences from the ward.

source: The retrospective datasets analysed in this study represent the first few months of the COVID-19 epidemic in the UK, and nosocomial transmission of the virus in the UK during this period has previously been reported at multiple sites (Meredith et al., 2020; Rickman et al., 2021; Carter et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a temporal description of the study context.

claim: Healthcare workers were at increased risk of infection and adverse health outcomes during the first wave of COVID-19 in the UK.
source: HCWs were at increased risk of infection and adverse health outcomes (Kursumovic et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020; The DELVE Initiative, 2020; Shah et al., 2020; Houlihan et al., 2020) and could have been important drivers of nosocomial transmission (Rivett et al., 2020).

evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and represents a speculative inference.

claim: The Sheffield dataset contained a large number of sequences obtained from HCWs, with population sequencing coverage for this group >80%.
source: Data were limited for Glasgow, but the Sheffield dataset contained a large number of sequences obtained from HCWs, with population sequencing coverage for this group >80%, and there was a close sequence match to at least one HCW observed for 87% of HOCIs.

claim: There was a close sequence match to at least one HCW observed for 87% of HOCIs in Sheffield.

claim: Healthcare workers were clearly linked into transmission networks within the hospital.
source: Our analysis has not evaluated direction of transmission to or from HCWs, but they were clearly linked into transmission networks within the hospital.

claim: A limitation of the current SRT approach is that it does not include detailed information regarding work locations for HCWs.

source: However, prospective use of the SRT would allow IPC teams to investigate linkage from a HOCI to any HCWs flagged as having a close sequence match.

claim: A phylogenetic approach is useful in excluding direct transmission between cases.
source: While a phylogenetic approach is useful in excluding direct transmission between cases, it can be more problematic to confirm transmission source (Volz and Frost, 2013).

source: While a phylogenetic approach is useful in excluding direct transmission between cases, it can be more problematic to confirm transmission source (Volz and Frost, 2013).

source: There have been advances in recent years in the computational efficiency and workflow standardisation possible for phylogenetic analyses that have made it easier to use these methods for real-time investigation of outbreaks, for example, through the development of the Nextstrain project (Hadfield et al., 2018; Huddleston et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There does not currently exist phylogenetic software for SARS-CoV-2 that produces reports or other outputs designed for direct and immediate use by IPC professionals.
source: However, there does not currently exist phylogenetic software for SARS-CoV-2 that produces reports or other outputs designed for direct and immediate use by IPC professionals.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of available tools, based on the authors' knowledge.

source: There will be cases in which phylogenetic analysis would provide information beyond that returned by the SRT, and the two approaches may be complementary to one another for outbreak investigation.

claim: Some clusters of genetically similar cases identified within a specific ward likely represented more than one transmission event onto the ward from similar viral lineages circulating within the healthcare system.
source: Comparison of SRT output to phylogenetic trees in a number of test cases suggested that some clusters of genetically similar cases identified within a specific ward likely represented more than one transmission event onto the ward from similar viral lineages circulating within the healthcare system.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparison of SRT output to phylogenetic trees.

claim: The presence of viruses within a ward or hospital that are genetically similar to a HOCI is considered evidence for nosocomial infection even when they are not plausible transmission sources themselves.
source: Whilst monophyletic clusters associated with a single location are easier to interpret, we consider the presence of viruses within a ward or hospital that are genetically similar to a HOCI as evidence for nosocomial infection even when they are not plausible transmission sources themselves, given the potential for asymptomatic transmission (He et al., 2020; Rivett et al., 2020; Oran and Topol, 2020; Lucey et al., 2021) and complex transmission networks (Meredith et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a methodological decision supported by citations about asymptomatic transmission and complex networks.

claim: The SRT uses a number of heuristic approximations in order to provide an integrated summary of epidemiological and sequence data.
source: The SRT uses a number of heuristic approximations in order to provide an integrated summary of epidemiological and sequence data.
evidence: This describes a methodological aspect of the SRT.

claim: The use of heuristic approximations is associated with the limitation that the SRT does not provide a full probabilistic model of potential transmission networks.
source: However, this choice is associated with the limitation that it does not provide a full probabilistic model of potential transmission networks.

source: The automated feedback provided by the SRT is nonetheless dependent on timely sequencing of a high proportion of viral samples from cases within the hospital concerned, ideally in combination with sequences also available from community-sampled cases.

claim: A reference set sequence is considered a close match to the focus sequence if there is a maximum of two SNP differences between them.
source: A reference set sequence is considered a close match to the focus sequence if there is a maximum of two SNP differences between them.

source: We use an expression of Bayes theorem to estimate probabilities for post-admission infection of each focus case divided by exposure on the unit, within the rest of the institution and from visitors (if allowed).

evidence: This describes the methodological approach of the SRT.

claim: In symptomatic focus cases, the prior probability is based on the time interval from admission to date of symptom onset or first positive test.
source: In symptomatic focus cases, we base Pprior on the time interval (t) from admission to date of symptom onset or first positive test (if date of symptom onset not recorded).

claim: The geographic weighting model was fitted separately for each study site using sequences strongly thought to represent community-acquired infection.
